steps.note: The Seventh Circuit holds that a federal Rule 23 action under a federal statute needs personal jurisdiction for the named plaintiff, without a separate showing for each absentee. This is a circuit holding, not a Supreme Court resolution of every class setting.
steps.effect: Limits Bristol-Myers in the Seventh Circuit

steps.note: Every class member who seeks damages must have standing; a statutory violation without concrete harm is not enough.

timelines.guide: Separate certification requirements, the constitutional ability to bind absentees, notice and individual standing. Arbitration limits and personal-jurisdiction questions are additional branches. Briseno and Mussat state circuit holdings rather than nationwide Supreme Court rules.

timelines.title: Summary judgment: from 'slightest doubt' to the 1986 trilogy
timelines.question: When is there no genuine dispute of material fact for a jury to decide?
timelines.anchor: how readily summary judgment is granted
timelines.now: Summary judgment is proper when, viewing the evidence for the nonmovant, no reasonable jury could find for that party under the trial burden of proof (Anderson); a movant without the burden may point to missing evidence (Celotex). Courts may not resolve genuine disputes for the movant (Tolan) unless the record blatantly contradicts one side (Scott).

steps.note: Summary judgment is improper if there is the slightest doubt about the facts, especially when a witness's credibility is at stake.
steps.fate: Its 'slightest doubt' standard was later abandoned

steps.note: The hope that a jury will disbelieve the other side's witnesses is not evidence; a party with the burden needs proof of its own.
Summary judgment should be used sparingly in complex antitrust cases where motive and intent matter and the proof lies with the other side.
When the facts turn on the motive and credibility of the movant's own witnesses, the opponent may test them by cross-examination at trial.
The movant must foreclose any genuine issue; if its own showing leaves a gap, the motion fails even without a response.
steps.fate: Narrowed by Celotex (1986)

steps.note: Evidence as consistent with lawful competition as with conspiracy cannot carry an implausible conspiracy claim to a jury.
A dispute is genuine only if a reasonable jury could find for the nonmovant under the burden of proof that applies at trial.

After adequate time for discovery, a movant without the trial burden may identify the absence of evidence on an essential element without negating it. Only after that initial showing must the opponent identify a genuine jury issue.
A court need not accept a version of events that the record, such as a video, so blatantly contradicts that no jury could believe it.
Courts must still credit the nonmovant's evidence and may not resolve genuine disputes for the movant, even in qualified-immunity cases.

timelines.guide: Follow the movant’s initial showing, the opponent’s evidentiary response and the trial burden of proof. The 1986 decisions permit judgment without a genuine jury issue; Scott does not authorize ordinary credibility weighing, and Tolan preserves the favorable view of disputed evidence.

timelines.title: Joinder: the same transaction or occurrence
timelines.question: When do claims and parties belong together in one suit?
timelines.anchor: what 'same transaction' covers
timelines.now: Rules 13 and 20 use related but different transaction tests; permissive party joinder also needs a common question of law or fact. Rules 20(b), 21 and 42(b) manage prejudice and complexity. Procedural joinder does not dispense with an independent or supplemental jurisdictional basis.

steps.note: Under the code, claims arising from one transaction may be joined though they fall in different categories, such as false imprisonment and slander.
'Transaction' is a flexible word: a counterclaim arises from it when logically related to the claim, though the facts differ.
Crossclaims and claims against added parties arise from the same transaction when logically related, with separate trials to manage them.
A counterclaim logically related to the claim is compulsory under Rule 13(a), and it comes within ancillary jurisdiction.
Plaintiffs may join when their claims arise from a series of logically related events and share a common question, as with a company-wide policy.

timelines.guide: The same-transaction formulations operate in different rules: compulsory counterclaims, crossclaims and permissive party joinder. Rule 20 also requires a common question. Procedural permission to join does not itself supply subject-matter jurisdiction.

timelines.title: Required parties: from indispensability to equity and good conscience
timelines.question: When must an absent person be joined, and what happens if that cannot be done?
timelines.anchor: when a case must stop for an absent party
timelines.now: Rule 19(a) first asks whether an absentee is required; if joinder is not feasible, Rule 19(b) weighs prejudice, ways to lessen it, the adequacy of a judgment without the absentee and the plaintiff's alternatives to decide whether the case goes on. Joint tortfeasors are not required parties (Temple), and an immune sovereign with a real stake can compel dismissal (Pimentel).

steps.note: An absentee is indispensable only if any decree would inevitably affect its interest; separable interests let the court proceed.
The rewritten Rule 19 drops fixed labels for a two-step test: who should be joined, then whether to go on without them.
Indispensability is the conclusion of a practical weighing of everyone's interests in equity and good conscience, not a label applied first.
Joint tortfeasors are permissive parties, not required ones, so Rule 19(b) is never reached for them.
Where an immune sovereign with a nonfrivolous claim cannot be joined and could be harmed, the action must ordinarily be dismissed.

timelines.guide: Apply Rule 19(a) before Rule 19(b). If joinder is required but infeasible, practical prejudice and available remedies determine whether to proceed; Temple stops at the first question, while Pimentel gives sovereign immunity special weight.

timelines.title: Interpleader: from the strict bill to minimal diversity
timelines.question: When can a stakeholder facing competing claims make the claimants contest them in one suit?
timelines.anchor: who may interplead whom
timelines.now: A stakeholder facing competing claims to one fund may interplead under Rule 22, with ordinary jurisdiction, or under § 1335, with minimal diversity among claimants and nationwide service, even when the claims are unliquidated and not yet reduced to judgment. Interpleader protects the fund; it does not force every related claim into one court (Tashire).

steps.note: Statutory interpleader requires adverse claimants with minimal diversity, a stake worth at least $500, and deposit of the stake or a qualifying bond. The 1936 Act broadens access; these conditions still matter.
A disinterested tenant may interplead its landlord and a rival claimant despite the rule that a tenant may not deny the landlord's title.
An insurer may interplead tort claimants whose claims may exceed its policy limit, though it denies liability and the claims are unliquidated.
Minimal diversity suffices and interpleader may come before judgment, but it protects only the fund and cannot force all claims into one court.

timelines.guide: Separate Rule 22 interpleader, which needs ordinary jurisdiction, from statutory interpleader under § 1335. The latter has a fund/deposit requirement and minimal diversity. Hancock is a California comparison; Tashire confines the injunction to protection of the stake.

timelines.title: Nondelegation: from contingency to the intelligible principle
timelines.question: How much lawmaking power can Congress hand to the executive?
timelines.anchor: what Congress may delegate
timelines.now: The intelligible-principle approach governs the selected majority decisions; Benzene and Gundy show competing rationales and proposals for stricter limits. FCC v. Consumers’ Research (2025) independently confirms sufficient congressional guidance and retained FCC control of the private administrator. That decision is checked in the audit trail but has no separate atlas brief here.

steps.note: Congress may make a law's revival turn on a fact the President finds and proclaims; that is not a transfer of lawmaking.
When Congress names the contingency and its consequence, the President who finds the fact acts as its agent, not as a lawmaker.
Congress may let an administrator fill in details by rule and make breaking those rules a crime that Congress itself defines and punishes.
The test is named: a delegation is valid if Congress lays down an intelligible principle to which the delegate must conform.
First invalidation: Congress let the President ban hot-oil shipments without stating a policy, a standard or the findings required.
Power to write binding codes for whole industries, guided only by general recovery aims, is an unconstitutional transfer of lawmaking.
Wartime price control stands: standards need only be definite enough for a court to tell whether Congress's will was obeyed.
A three-judge court upholds the wage-price freeze: text, purpose, history and implied limits can supply the standard; breadth alone is no defect.
A plurality reads the OSH Act narrowly to avoid a sweeping delegation; Justice Rehnquist alone would hold the delegation unconstitutional.
The Sentencing Commission passes the intelligible-principle test; only Scalia objects to lawmaking by a body with no other power to exercise.
An agency cannot cure a standardless delegation by limiting itself; 'requisite to protect the public health' is a sufficient principle.

Four Justices uphold the delegation after narrowing SORNA by interpretation. Alito supplies the fifth vote under existing doctrine while inviting reconsideration; three dissenters propose a stricter approach. No majority replaces the intelligible-principle test.

timelines.guide: Distinguish finding a statutory contingency from filling administrative details and exercising delegated discretion. The 1935 invalidations are exceptions to the intelligible-principle approach. Benzene and Gundy contain separate rationales, not majority decisions replacing that test.

timelines.title: Congress after it legislates: no veto, no officers of its own
timelines.question: Once Congress delegates, may it keep a hand in executing the law?
timelines.anchor: Congress's control after it legislates
timelines.now: Congress controls execution by passing laws through both Houses and presentment, by funding and oversight, and through the Senate's roles in confirmation and impeachment; it may not veto by resolution or appoint or remove (other than by impeachment) officers who execute the law.

steps.note: The Senate may not share in removing an executive officer; a statute making removal depend on its consent is invalid.
Congress may not appoint officers who enforce the law; officials it names may only gather information and investigate, as a committee could.
A one-House veto is lawmaking: once it delegates, Congress may alter the delegate's power only by bicameral passage and presentment.
Congress may not keep removal power, short of impeachment, over an officer who executes the law, because removal brings control.
The D.C. Circuit holds that Congress's own agents may not sit on an enforcement agency, even as nonvoting members.

timelines.guide: Congress may legislate and oversee, but appointing or controlling officials who execute the law is a different act. Chadha concerns legislative effect outside Congress; Bowsher and FEC v. NRA concern control through officers rather than a legislative veto.

timelines.title: Presidential removal power
timelines.question: Can Congress protect officers from removal by the President?
timelines.anchor: the President's power to remove officers at will
timelines.now: Slaughter holds the FTC’s executive-power commissioners removable at will and overrules Humphrey’s to that extent; it leaves the Federal Reserve and non-Article III courts aside. Cook separately denies a stay and requires statutory removal process for a Fed Governor. Inferior-officer and adjudicative settings must not be generalized from the FTC holding.

steps.note: When Congress vests an inferior officer's appointment in a department head, it may also restrict that officer's removal.
The President's power to remove officers he appoints with Senate consent is his alone; Congress may not make it depend on the Senate.
Congress may protect members of a quasi-legislative, quasi-judicial commission such as the FTC from removal except for cause.
steps.fate: Overruled by Trump v. Slaughter (2026)

steps.note: The President may not remove a member of an adjudicatory body like the War Claims Commission merely to put his own appointee in its place, even when the statute says nothing about removal.
Congress may not keep for itself the power to remove an officer who executes the law; impeachment is its only removal tool.
The test turns functional: a good-cause limit on an inferior officer is valid unless it impedes the President's constitutional duties.
steps.fate: Confined by Seila Law (2020) to inferior officers with limited duties

steps.note: Two layers of for-cause protection between the President and officers who exercise executive power violate Article II.
A lone agency head wielding significant executive power may not be shielded; exceptions stay with multimember bodies and some inferior officers.

Seila’s single-director rule reaches the FHFA. Because the officer was properly appointed, the unconstitutional removal restriction does not automatically invalidate past actions; retrospective relief requires compensable harm caused by the restriction.
Humphrey's Executor overruled: FTC commissioners exercise executive power and must be removable at will; the Federal Reserve is reserved.

The Court denies a stay of Cook’s preliminary protection: removal is reviewable and the statute requires notice and an opportunity to respond. It treats the Federal Reserve’s history separately and leaves the precise definition of cause open.
steps.effect: Preserves the Fed separately at the stay stage

timelines.guide: Read each holding against the officer’s functions and structure. Myers bars Senate control, Humphrey’s protected the historical FTC, and later cases cut back insulation. Slaughter changes that precedent in 2026; Cook addresses the Federal Reserve separately at the stay stage.

timelines.title: Appointments: who is an officer, and who appoints whom
timelines.question: Who is an officer, and who may appoint whom?
timelines.anchor: who counts as an officer and how far the President's appointment power runs
timelines.now: A continuing position exercising significant federal authority is an office. Principal officers ordinarily require presidential nomination and Senate consent; Congress may vest an inferior officer’s appointment in the President alone, a court of law or a department head. Edmond and Arthrex concern supervision and review; recess appointments follow a separate clause.

steps.note: Congress may add duties germane to an existing office without requiring a fresh appointment of the officer who holds it.
Anyone exercising significant authority under federal law is an officer, appointed only as Article II allows; Congress may not appoint.
An independent counsel, removable for cause and limited in duties, jurisdiction and tenure, is an inferior officer whom a court may appoint.
Tax Court special trial judges are officers, not employees, and the Tax Court is a 'Court of Law' that may appoint them.
Assuming Shoemaker's germaneness principle applies, commissioned officers need no second appointment to serve as military judges, a duty germane to their office.
Inferior officers are those directed and supervised by Senate-confirmed officers; significant authority marks an officer, not a principal one.
The recess route is bounded: the Senate is in session when it says it is, and a break of under ten days is presumptively too short.
SEC administrative law judges are officers under Freytag, so appointment by staff was invalid; the cure is a new hearing before another official.
An inferior officer may not issue final decisions that no principal officer can review; the PTO Director must be able to review the Board.

timelines.guide: Officer status, principal-versus-inferior status and the permissible appointing authority are separate questions. Shoemaker and Weiss address new duties for an already appointed officer; Noel Canning addresses the separate recess-appointment route.

timelines.title: Presidential power: with, without and against Congress
timelines.question: Where does the President's power to act come from, and what limits it?
timelines.anchor: what the President may do without or against Congress
timelines.now: Courts sort presidential action by Justice Jackson's Youngstown framework: power is greatest with Congress's authorization, uncertain where Congress is silent (where long acquiescence can count), and weakest against its will. Statutes granting emergency powers are read for their stated predicates.

steps.note: Political discretion belongs to the executive, but a specific legal duty on which a person's rights depend can be enforced in court.
Where Congress has said how a law is to be executed, executive instructions cannot authorize more or shield the officer who obeys them.
The duty to execute the laws implies no power to dispense with them; a court may compel an officer's ministerial duty by mandamus.
Executive duties may be implied from the Constitution and general statutes, such as protecting a federal judge, not only from express laws.

Without a statute specifically authorizing the suit, but resting on Congress's commerce and postal legislation, the national government may sue in equity to stop forcible obstruction of interstate commerce and the mails.
Long executive practice known to Congress and left undisturbed implies its consent, here to the President's withdrawal of public lands.
The steel seizure fails: power must come from statute or the Constitution; Jackson's concurrence sorts action by Congress's will.
steps.effect: Rejects seizure; Jackson supplies a framework

steps.note: Jackson's categories become a spectrum: congressional acquiescence supports suspending claims, though the President has no plenary settlement power.
At the stay stage, the Guard statute likely requires lawful authority to use the regular military, which an asserted protective power did not supply.

timelines.guide: Distinguish a specific statutory duty, implied executive authority and action inconsistent with Congress. Youngstown’s holding rejects the seizure; Jackson’s three categories come from his concurrence and inform Dames & Moore’s narrower foreign-affairs holding.

timelines.title: Deference to agency interpretation, from Gray v. Powell to Loper Bright
timelines.question: How much weight does an agency's reading of a statute get in court?
timelines.anchor: how much weight agency interpretations get
timelines.now: Courts decide what a statute means for themselves (Loper Bright), giving an agency's view the weight its reasoning earns and policing any discretion Congress expressly delegated; earlier Chevron-based holdings keep their stare decisis effect, and Kisor's narrowed Auer deference still governs an agency's reading of its own regulations.

steps.note: When Congress leaves an agency to apply a term like 'producer' to particular facts, a reasoned application after a fair hearing stands.
The Board's application of 'employee' is accepted if it has warrant in the record and a reasonable basis in law.
steps.fate: Its 'employee' ruling was overridden by the Taft-Hartley Act (1947), which excluded independent contractors

steps.note: Agency interpretations do not bind courts but carry weight from their care, reasoning, consistency and power to persuade.
Two steps: if Congress spoke to the precise question, that controls; if the statute is silent or ambiguous, a permissible agency reading wins.
steps.fate: Overruled by Loper Bright (2024)

steps.note: Step zero: Chevron applies only where Congress gave power to act with the force of law and the agency used it; otherwise Skidmore.
steps.fate: Its Chevron threshold lapsed with Loper Bright (2024); Skidmore respect remains

steps.note: A court's earlier reading yields to a later reasonable agency reading unless the court held that the statute was unambiguous.
steps.fate: Fell with Chevron in Loper Bright (2024)

steps.note: Chevron applies even when the ambiguity concerns the scope of the agency's own authority.
steps.fate: Fell with Chevron in Loper Bright (2024)

steps.note: A question of deep economic and political significance is not implicitly left to the agency; the Court reads the statute itself.
Auer (Seminole Rock) deference to an agency's reading of its own rule survives, but only for genuine ambiguity and an authoritative, expert reading.
Chevron overruled: under APA § 706 courts decide what statutes mean independently, honoring real delegations and giving agency views Skidmore weight.

timelines.guide: Skidmore persuasion and historical Chevron deference to statutes are different routes. Loper Bright rejects ambiguity-based Chevron deference while respecting genuine delegations and prior holdings. Kisor concerns an agency’s own regulation, a separate interpretive branch.

timelines.title: Major questions: clear authorization for vast power
timelines.question: When does an agency need clear congressional authorization?
timelines.anchor: how much the major-questions doctrine demands of agencies
timelines.now: When an agency claims power of vast economic and political significance, it must point to clear congressional authorization, not merely a plausible reading of general words. Justices still differ on whether the doctrine is a substantive clear-statement rule or, as Justice Barrett puts it, ordinary reading of text in context.

steps.note: Absent a clear mandate, the plurality will not read the OSH Act to give the agency unprecedented power over American industry.
In extraordinary cases courts hesitate to find an implicit delegation over a large part of the economy; Congress had not given the FDA power to regulate tobacco products as customarily marketed.
A question of deep economic and political significance was not left to the IRS; the Court decides it by reading the whole statute.
A nationwide eviction moratorium needs clear authorization; a general disease-control power read with its narrow examples does not give it.
A vaccine-or-test mandate for large employers is a general public-health measure, not an occupational standard Congress clearly authorized.
The same day, a vaccination rule for health-care staff stands: it falls within express power to protect patients' health and safety.
The doctrine is named: in extraordinary cases the agency must point to clear congressional authorization; a merely plausible reading is not enough.
Power to 'waive or modify' allows modest changes, not mass loan cancellation; Barrett recasts the doctrine as reading text in context.

timelines.guide: These cases restrict extraordinary assertions of agency authority, but do not invalidate every large program. Biden v. Missouri is a statutory-authorization contrast. Benzene and the emergency cases must be read with their plurality or interim posture.

timelines.title: Protected interests: from privilege to entitlement
timelines.question: When is a government job or benefit liberty or property that due process protects?
timelines.anchor: what counts as a protected interest
timelines.now: Due process protects a legitimate claim of entitlement defined by law or mutual understanding (Roth), whatever the privilege label; once the interest exists, the Constitution, not the statute that created it, sets the minimum process (Loudermill), and unrestricted official discretion can defeat the entitlement.

steps.note: Government employment is a privilege, not property, so dismissal needs no due process; an equally divided Court affirmed in 1951.
steps.fate: Its right/privilege premise was rejected in Roth (1972)

steps.note: Officials may not cost a person a private job through a clearance hearing without confrontation unless Congress or the President expressly allows it.
No hearing was due to bar a cook from a naval base: the process due depends on the government function and the private interest at stake.
Welfare benefits are a statutory entitlement, not a privilege, so ending them triggers due process and a prior hearing.
Property means a legitimate claim of entitlement from an independent source such as state law; a one-year appointment gives none.
Mutually explicit understandings, not only formal tenure, can create a property interest in continued public employment.
A three-Justice plurality says a statute granting a job may also limit its procedures, the 'bitter with the sweet'; six Justices disagree.
steps.fate: Rejected by the Court in Loudermill (1985)
steps.effect: Splits over statutory control of process

steps.note: State law creates the interest, but the Constitution sets the procedure for taking it away; the bitter-with-the-sweet idea is rejected.
Meeting eligibility criteria is no entitlement when supply is limited and officials have unrestricted discretion over who gets the benefit.
A Colorado court holds that a no-entitlement clause does not defeat a property interest where officials cannot deny funded benefits to the eligible.

timelines.guide: First identify protected liberty or property; then ask what process is due. Roth rejects the privilege label as the test but requires an entitlement source. Loudermill rejects the Arnett plurality’s attempt to let the source statute set the constitutional procedure.

timelines.title: What process is due, and when
timelines.question: When is a hearing due, and what kind?
timelines.anchor: how much process is due
timelines.now: Mathews balancing decides what process is due once a protected interest is at stake: a general rule needs no individual hearing (Bi-Metallic), and otherwise notice and a chance to respond scale with the interest, the risk of error and the government's burden; an informal chance to respond followed by a fuller hearing or an ordinary lawsuit often suffices.

steps.note: When a body assesses particular owners on individual grounds, each must get notice and a hearing with argument and proof.
A general rule applied to everyone alike needs no individual hearing; the check on it is political, not procedural.
Welfare may not be cut off before an evidentiary hearing with oral presentation, confrontation and an impartial decisionmaker.
Three-factor balancing of private interest, risk of error and government burden; no evidentiary hearing is needed before disability benefits stop.
School paddling implicates liberty, but common-law limits and later civil and criminal remedies supply the process due; no prior hearing.
A customer facing a utility shutoff must be told how to dispute the bill and get a chance to present it to someone able to fix it.
Before firing a tenured employee: notice, an explanation of the evidence and a chance to respond, with a fuller hearing afterward.
Before an order reinstating a whistleblower, the employer gets the substance of the evidence and a chance to respond, not a trial-type hearing.
Mathews, modified to weigh the plaintiff's interest, governs private prejudgment attachment; attaching a home without notice or exigency fails.
After a lawful seizure the owner must be told of it, but not of return remedies set out in published statutes and cases.
Where an ordinary contract suit can fully protect a disputed claim for payment, that suit is all the process due.

timelines.guide: First distinguish general policymaking from a decision about particular persons. Where an individual protected interest is affected, compare timing and safeguards under Mathews. A statutory hearing right can exist independently of constitutional due process.

timelines.title: Agency adjudication, public rights and the civil jury
timelines.question: When may Congress send a claim to an agency instead of a jury in an Article III court?
timelines.anchor: what Congress may send to an agency without a jury
timelines.now: Jarkesy requires an Article III jury for the SEC fraud penalties before it, a legal claim analogous to common-law fraud. It distinguishes Atlas Roofing rather than abolishing agency adjudication. Article III authority, public-rights exceptions and the particular claim and remedy require separate examination.

steps.note: Matters of public right, like summary collection of a revenue officer's debt, may be settled by the executive without an Article III trial.
When the Government enforces new statutory public rights, Congress may assign penalty cases to an agency forum with no jury.
steps.fate: Distinguished, not overruled, in Jarkesy (2024)

steps.note: A government suit for civil penalties is legal in nature, so the defendant gets a jury on liability, though the judge sets the amount.
Calling a claim a core proceeding cannot strip the jury right; a traditional legal claim against a stranger to the estate is no public right.

SEC fraud penalties resemble a common-law legal claim and require an Article III jury. The Court distinguishes Atlas Roofing rather than overruling it; public rights and other kinds of agency adjudication remain separate questions.

timelines.guide: Article III adjudication and the Seventh Amendment jury right are related but distinct. A new statutory label does not settle either. Jarkesy addresses SEC fraud penalties; it distinguishes Atlas Roofing and does not abolish every administrative adjudication.

timelines.title: Reasoned decisionmaking: the agency's own reasons and the hard look
timelines.question: How closely do courts review an agency's reasons?
timelines.anchor: how demanding review of agency reasoning is
timelines.now: The agency must give legally adequate reasons on the record, consider material factors and relevant reliance, and answer significant comments. Chenery ordinarily requires remand rather than substitute judicial policy reasoning; Fox does not impose a heightened standard simply because policy changes. Ohio v. EPA assesses likely error on an interim stay record.

steps.note: A court judges an agency order only on the grounds the agency invoked; it may not supply a policy judgment the agency never made.
The concise statement of basis and purpose need not answer every comment but must show the major issues and why the agency chose as it did.
Courts ask whether the agency took a 'hard look' and engaged in reasoned decisionmaking; if it did, they defer even if they would differ.
Review is searching and careful, on the full administrative record: did the agency weigh the relevant factors, or make a clear error of judgment?
A discretionary requirement fails when the agency does not tie it to the statute's goal or answer concrete objections in the record.
An agency may base standards on predicted technology if it answers objections and gives plausible reasons each remaining step can be done in time.
The core test: examine the data and connect facts to choice; rescinding a rule gets the same review, and counsel's later reasons do not count.
After State Farm's remand, the new passive-restraint rule's present choices survive as reasonably explained; its contingent parts are unripe.
A policy change needs no better reasons than the old policy: acknowledge the change, give good reasons, and address reliance and prior findings.
The stated reason must be the real one: when the explanation does not match the record, the action goes back to the agency.
Rescinding a program requires weighing reliance and alternatives within it; reasons offered later cannot save the original action.

A legal error in an agency’s discretionary reasoning ordinarily requires Chenery remand; the court may not simply substitute its own corrected analysis. Narrow remand exceptions are not a general license to supply agency policy.
Failing to respond to a significant comment likely makes a rule arbitrary and capricious, and that defect can support a stay.
steps.effect: Finds a likely defect at the stay stage

timelines.guide: The line concerns whether the agency supplied legally adequate reasons on the relevant record. Chenery limits substitute judicial rationales; State Farm governs rescission; Fox explains policy changes; Ohio v. EPA is an interim assessment on a stay application.

timelines.title: Substantial-evidence review of agency findings
timelines.question: How much factual support must an agency finding have?
timelines.anchor: what the substantial-evidence standard demands
timelines.now: An agency finding stands if a reasonable mind could accept the evidence as adequate on the whole record, including evidence that cuts against it; the same quantum of support applies to informal action under arbitrary-and-capricious review, and the bar is not high.

steps.note: Substantial evidence is judged on the whole record, including evidence that detracts from the finding and the examiner's contrary report.
Examining physicians' written reports can be substantial evidence despite hearsay and contrary testimony when the claimant could have subpoenaed them.
Substantial-evidence and arbitrary-and-capricious review demand the same factual support; the former simply confines it to a formal record.
A health standard may rest on cumulative, imperfect science, but the agency must show with evidence why a feasible added protection is unneeded.
An agency must apply the standard it announces; a finding that quietly demands more than that standard lacks substantial evidence.
The APA's standards govern review of the patent office's fact findings; the stricter clear-error test courts apply to judges does not.
Informal action needs the same evidentiary support as formal action, drawn from what the agency had before it when it acted.
The threshold is not high and is applied case by case; an expert's refusal to share underlying data does not automatically defeat it.

timelines.guide: This is review of factual support, not independent judicial factfinding. Whole-record review includes evidence against the agency. ADAPSO’s equation of evidentiary support does not erase procedural differences or make every statutory review provision identical.

timelines.title: Reviewing agency inaction and enforcement choices
timelines.question: When may a court review an agency's decision not to act?
timelines.anchor: when agency inaction is reviewable
timelines.now: A refusal to enforce is presumptively unreviewable (Heckler), but denials of rulemaking petitions are reviewable with great deference, rescinding a program that confers benefits is reviewable, and a court can compel only a discrete action the law requires (Norton).

steps.note: 'Committed to agency discretion' is a narrow exception for cases with no law to apply; statutory standards make action reviewable.
A decision not to sue to set aside a union election is reviewable, but only for rationality, on the Secretary's statement of reasons.
A refusal to enforce is presumptively unreviewable unless the statute supplies guidelines that limit the agency's enforcement discretion.
A refusal to begin rulemaking is reviewable under a highly deferential standard but still needs a reasoned, record-supported explanation.
A court may compel only a discrete action the agency is legally required to take, not general compliance with a broad mandate.
Denying a rulemaking petition is reviewable, and the agency's reasons must track the statute's criteria, not unrelated policy preferences.
Ending a program that solicits applications and grants benefits is more than passive nonenforcement, so Heckler's presumption does not bar review.

timelines.guide: Do not treat all inaction alike. Enforcement refusal, denial of a rulemaking petition, rescission of a benefits program and failure to perform a mandatory discrete duty follow distinct review routes.

timelines.title: Rule or order: the agency's choice of procedure
timelines.question: May an agency make policy case by case instead of by rule?
timelines.anchor: the agency's freedom to choose rule or adjudication
timelines.now: Chenery II and Bell Aerospace generally permit a statutorily authorized agency to choose policymaking by adjudication, subject to abuse and unfair retroactivity concerns. Wyman-Gordon has a divided rationale. National Petroleum’s rulemaking holding concerns the FTC statute and later statutory procedures, not an unrestricted power for every agency.

steps.note: The APA sorts agency action into two kinds, each with its own procedure: rules, which have future effect, and orders, the products of adjudication.
The choice between a general rule and case-by-case adjudication is primarily the agency's; retroactive effect is weighed, not fatal.
No majority: a plurality says a purely prospective rule announced in adjudication evades the APA, but the order against the party is enforced.
steps.effect: Specific order upheld; rule rationale divided

steps.note: The D.C. Circuit reads the FTC Act’s general rulemaking clause to authorize binding rules defining unfair or deceptive practices. The holding concerns that statutory scheme, not every agency’s general rulemaking clause.
steps.fate: Congress confirmed the power for unfair or deceptive practices but imposed hybrid procedures in the Magnuson-Moss Act (1975)

steps.note: The Board may announce new principles through adjudication; the choice is reviewed only for abuse, as where it would upset reliance.

timelines.guide: An agency needs statutory authority for either tool. Chenery II and Bell Aerospace generally leave the choice to the agency; Wyman-Gordon splits over an announced prospective rule while sustaining the specific order. National Petroleum interprets the FTC statute.

timelines.title: Rulemaking procedure: formal hearings, notice and comment, and the limits on courts
timelines.question: How much procedure must an agency use to make a rule, and may courts demand more?
timelines.anchor: what procedure rulemaking must follow
timelines.now: Section 553 is the ordinary notice-and-comment framework, subject to its exemptions and the governing statute. Formal rulemaking has a distinct on-the-record trigger; Marathon Oil concerns formal adjudication. Courts enforce meaningful notice, participation and reasons while Vermont Yankee limits added procedures. Mock addresses a particular proposal at a preliminary stage.

steps.note: The APA requires notice, written comment and a statement of basis and purpose; trial-type procedure only when rules must be made on the record.
In on-the-record rulemaking, parties must be able to test the data behind the agency's summaries, or the findings lack support.
Formal rulemaking applies only when a statute calls for rules 'on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing' or the like.
Even short of formal procedure, a rule under substantial-evidence review needs a record whose factual premises parties could test.

A separate adjudication branch: the Ninth Circuit reads a statutory “public hearing” on disputed facts to trigger formal APA adjudication without “on the record.” This does not expand formal rulemaking under Florida East Coast.
Notice must disclose the scientific data behind a proposal, and the final statement must answer comments that go to the rule's core.
Courts may not add procedures to informal rulemaking beyond those the Constitution, the APA and the governing statute require.
The disclosure rule survives Vermont Yankee: studies the agency relies on must be released for comment; Judge Kavanaugh questions it.
Vermont Yankee applied: interpretive rules need no notice and comment, even when they change an earlier interpretation.
Courts may not add an open-mindedness test to notice and comment; the APA's objective requirements, if met, are enough.
A final rule must be a logical outgrowth of the proposal; the Fifth Circuit held the pistol-brace rule was not, so its challengers were likely to succeed.
steps.effect: Finds likely notice failure on this proposal

timelines.guide: Informal notice and comment, formal rulemaking and formal adjudication have different triggers. Marathon Oil concerns adjudication, not an exception that makes ordinary rulemaking formal. Vermont Yankee limits added procedures while courts interpret the APA’s existing duties.

timelines.title: Guidance documents: legislative rule, interpretive rule or policy statement
timelines.question: When must an agency use notice and comment for a document it calls guidance?
timelines.anchor: when guidance must go through notice and comment
timelines.now: Binding legal effect or creation of new law can make guidance a legislative rule; a genuine interpretation or nonbinding policy statement follows a different route. Perez rejects extra notice-and-comment requirements merely for changing an interpretation. Circuit tests and statutory exceptions still require attention to the specific document.

steps.note: A policy statement only announces what the agency intends; not being a binding norm, it is exempt, but must be defended each time it is applied.
A pronouncement with present binding effect that leaves the agency no real discretion is a legislative rule, whatever its label.

The D.C. Circuit lists indicia of legislative rules: an independent enforcement basis, CFR publication, express legislative authority or amendment of a legislative rule. Later cases focus on legal effect; publication alone is not a universal conclusive test.
A requirement that cannot be derived from a regulation by interpretation, such as a flat eight-foot fence height, is legislative.
Guidance explaining a duty within a regulation is interpretive, but a definitive interpretation may not be fundamentally revised without comment.
steps.fate: Its rule on revising interpretations was abrogated by Perez (2015)

steps.note: Guidance that states a settled position and binds in practice is reviewable final action and cannot expand a rule without rulemaking.
A document labeled guidance is a legislative rule when its text binds both the regulated parties and the agency itself.
The Paralyzed Veterans revision rule is abrogated: interpretive rules are exempt from notice and comment whether new or changed.
A deferred-action program that in practice leaves officials no real discretion is likely a substantive rule needing notice and comment.
A rule is interpretive only if the statute or rule it explains compels or logically justifies it; guidance that makes new law is legislative.

timelines.guide: An interpretation or policy statement differs from a rule with legal force. Older circuit criteria and practical-binding tests must be read in context; Perez abrogates the extra procedure for revising an interpretation rather than authorizing disguised legislative rules.

timelines.title: Article III standing: injury, traceability, redress
timelines.question: Who has a case or controversy to bring to federal court?
timelines.anchor: how readily a plaintiff has standing
timelines.now: Article III requires concrete, particularized and actual or imminent injury, traceability and likely redressability. For intangible damages injuries, TransUnion uses historical analogues and rejects unmaterialized risk alone; physical and financial injuries remain ordinary examples. United States v. Texas addresses demands for more third-party arrests, not every challenge to enforcement policy.

steps.note: The threshold becomes injury in fact, economic or otherwise, replacing the older demand for an established legal interest.
Aesthetic and environmental harm counts as injury, but the plaintiff or its members must suffer it; concern for a cause is not enough.
Injury must be concrete, particularized and imminent, traceable and redressable; a citizen-suit provision cannot dispense with it.
Legislators lack standing for an abstract dilution of institutional power, and a statute authorizing their suit cannot supply the injury.
Denial of information a statute requires to be disclosed is a concrete injury, even though many voters share it.
Reasonable concerns that curtail use of a river are injury, and civil penalties paid to the Treasury redress it by deterrence.
States get special solicitude: a threatened coastline and a procedural right let Massachusetts challenge EPA's refusal to regulate.
Injury must be concrete as well as particularized; a bare procedural violation of a statute is not automatically enough.
A provision with no penalty and no enforcement causes no traceable injury, so the individual and state challengers lacked standing.

Every member recovering damages needs concrete injury. For intangible injury the Court asks for a close historical analogue; an unmaterialized risk alone does not support retrospective damages, though prospective relief is a separate inquiry.
States' indirect costs give them no judicially cognizable interest in forcing the Executive to make more arrests.

timelines.guide: Keep injury, traceability and redressability separate. ADAPSO also discusses the statutory zone of interests, traced elsewhere. TransUnion restricts damages standing for unmaterialized risk; it does not turn every physical or financial injury into a historical-analogue inquiry.

timelines.title: Statutory standing: the zone of interests
timelines.question: Whose interests let them sue to enforce a statute against an agency?
timelines.anchor: how wide the zone of interests is
timelines.now: APA review asks whether the plaintiff’s interest is arguably within the relevant provision’s zone, a lenient inquiry distinct from Article III. The formulation for another statutory cause of action may differ. Lexmark treats the issue as statutory authorization to sue, not a jurisdictional or free-floating prudential limit.

steps.note: Responsible representatives of the listening public, not only economic competitors, may intervene to contest a broadcast license renewal.
Beyond injury, the plaintiff's interest need only be arguably within the zone of interests the statute protects or regulates.
The zone test is not demanding: it bars only interests so marginal to the statute that Congress cannot be assumed to have meant them to sue.
The zone is set by the statute whose violation is claimed; postal workers' job interests fall outside the postal monopoly laws.
An agency's policy interest does not make it 'adversely affected or aggrieved'; the Director could not appeal a worker's award.
The zone is drawn from the particular provision invoked, and economic interests in avoiding needless regulation can fall within it.
A plaintiff need not show that Congress meant to benefit it; banks are arguably within the zone of a credit-union membership limit.
Title VII's 'person aggrieved' means the zone of interests, which covers an employee fired to punish a co-worker's charge.
The test is lenient: a neighbor's economic, environmental and aesthetic interests are arguably within a land-acquisition statute.
Interests that align with a statute's beneficiaries only by accident, as paper sellers' do under securities law, fall outside the zone.

timelines.guide: Article III standing and authorization to sue under a statute are separate questions. The APA uses an especially lenient zone test; another statutory cause of action may use a different formulation. Lexmark treats this as statutory interpretation, not subject-matter jurisdiction.

timelines.title: Organizations as plaintiffs
timelines.question: When may an organization sue for its members, or for itself?
timelines.anchor: when an organization may sue
timelines.now: An association may sue for its members if at least one identified member has standing, the interests are germane to its purpose and individual participation is not required (a prudential prong Congress may waive); an organization suing for itself needs its own concrete injury, and Havens is read narrowly (FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, 2024).

steps.note: An organization may sue for members who are themselves injured; its long-standing interest in a cause does not give it standing.
An organization has standing in its own right when the defendant's practices perceptibly impair its services and drain its resources.
steps.fate: Held to its context by FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine (2024)

steps.note: Hunt's three-part test for associational standing is reaffirmed, and a class action is not a required substitute for it.
Conflicts among members do not defeat associational standing, but the members represented must themselves have standing.
Hunt's third prong is prudential, not constitutional, so Congress may let a union sue for its members' damages.
A genuine voluntary membership organization that meets Hunt has standing; its members need not also control or fund it.

timelines.guide: An organization suing for members differs from one claiming its own injury. Hunt’s framework governs the former; Havens concerns the latter. FDA v. Alliance narrows diversion-of-resources reasoning and does not collapse the two routes.

timelines.title: Text, purpose and legislative history
timelines.question: How far may a court look beyond the words of a statute?
timelines.anchor: the role of purpose and legislative history against text
timelines.now: The Court begins, and usually ends, with ordinary meaning read in context, aided by structure, canons and presumptions; legislative history and purpose may confirm a reading but rarely override clear text, a sharp change from Holy Trinity.

steps.note: General words of a statute yield to its purpose and to the maxim that no one may profit from his own wrong: the murderer does not inherit.
A case within the letter may fall outside the statute when its history, context and consequences show the legislature did not mean it.
Legislative history may be consulted even when the words of a statute seem clear on first reading.
When a literal reading gives odd results and raises constitutional doubts, purpose and history support a narrower reading of 'utilized'.
Textualism gains ground: 'attorney's fee' does not include expert fees, and courts may not supplement clear text with purpose.
steps.fate: Partly overridden by the Civil Rights Act of 1991, which allows expert fees in § 1981 and § 1981a suits

steps.note: The Second Circuit finds 'any court' ambiguous in context and, relying on legislative history, reads it to exclude foreign convictions.
The Court reaches the same result by presuming that Congress legislates with domestic concerns in mind; three Justices dissent on the text.
Text controls over a conference report: a fee condition on federal funds needs clear notice, and legislative history cannot supply it.
Ordinary meaning and mechanics decide: a bump stock does not fire more than one shot by a single function of the trigger.
Ordinary meaning cuts both ways: some parts kits and unfinished frames are covered, so the agency's rule is not facially invalid.

timelines.guide: These decisions show competing uses of text, context, purpose and history, not a steady replacement of one method. Riggs is a New York decision; the federal cases interpret different statutes, and constitutional or clear-notice principles can affect their reasoning.

timelines.title: Words known by their company: ejusdem generis and noscitur a sociis
timelines.question: How do the words around a term limit what it means?
timelines.anchor: how far the associated-words canons narrow general terms
timelines.now: Courts read an ambiguous term in light of its neighbors (noscitur a sociis) and a catchall in light of the specific items before it (ejusdem generis), but these canons give way when text, structure or purpose points the other way.

steps.note: 'Vehicle' after a list of land vehicles means things that move on land, and a criminal law must give fair warning; airplanes are out.
Ejusdem generis: 'other dangerous weapon' after dagger, dirk and stiletto reaches stabbing weapons, not a rifle.
Noscitur a sociis and consistent usage: 'communication' in the prospectus definition means public solicitations, not a private sale contract.
The Second Circuit reads 'negligent transmission' with 'loss' and 'miscarriage': it covers harm to the mail, not injury from a misplaced package.
The Court resolves the circuit split the same way: the postal exception covers mail lost, late, damaged or misdelivered, not every delivery mishap.
Ejusdem generis limits the NLRA's 'other concerted activities' to things like organizing and bargaining, not class procedures.

timelines.guide: The canons are contextual tools, not mechanical commands to narrow every general word. Each case identifies the relevant grouping and statutory setting; Dolan resolves the postal-exception split, while Epic also addresses the FAA and NLRA’s interaction.

contracts.why: The only express-warranty case on the map; it applies UCC § 2-313 to sales talk and brochure figures, with no line of cases in the course.
States the settled presumption against legal intent in domestic arrangements; no other case on the map develops it.
A small-claims application of New York's dating-service statute (GBL § 394-c); statutory consumer protection, not a developing contract doctrine.
The only noncompete case on the map; its own turn (Wyoming abandoning the blue pencil it adopted in 1993) is internal to one state.
Illegality defense applied to a seller who furthered the buyer's improper use; with X.L.O. it forms no line, as the two decide different points.
Contract tainted by an antitrust conspiracy, enforced unless the judgment would enforce the unlawful conduct itself; a one-off public-policy point.

civpro.why: Applies a Missouri rule that special damages be specifically pleaded; the course has no line of cases on special damages.
Applies notice pleading and the rule that a conditional privilege is an affirmative defense; it adds no step to the pleading line.
One-off point that a statutory damages cap is an affirmative defense under Rule 8(c), waived if not raised; no line among the course's cases.
Applies Rule 8(b)'s requirements for answers; no development through a line of cases.
Applies Rule 14 to a contingent claim over; impleader has no line of development among the course's cases.
A plurality reading of the 1966 intervention rule; the rest of the intervention line runs only through supporting cases.
Applies a Kansas real-party-in-interest statute to a subrogated insurer; no line of cases on Rule 17 in the course.
Settles one point about appeals from consolidated cases; the finality and collateral-order line runs through supporting cases, not map cases.

lrs.why: Political-question ruling on partisan gerrymandering; its line (Baker v. Carr, Vieth) is not among the course's cases, and it is not an administrative-law doctrine.
The course's only Recess Appointments Clause decision; its sole companion is the Third Circuit's New Vista ruling, too thin for a line, and it does not concern who is an officer.
Statutory comparative-hearing right for mutually exclusive license applicants; no line of development among the course's cases (Church of Christ is placed with statutory standing).
